boards.title: Only Happens Here: 10 Traditions That Make No Sense Anywhere Else
boards.description: Ten documented UH Mānoa traditions spanning commencement, cultural recognition, law-school rituals, and Rainbow history.

cards.title: Watch for the Rainbow
cards.subtitle: UH Athletics origin story
cards.notes: At a game, look skyward with the crowd: UH Athletics records the long-running belief that a rainbow over a game means Hawaiʻi will not lose.
cards.short_summary: A 1923 football-game rainbow became a lasting UH good-luck legend.
cards.evidence_claim: UH Athletics says reporters began calling UH teams the Rainbows after a 1923 game and that a tradition arose that Hawaiʻi would not lose when a rainbow appeared.
cards.access_notes: A historical athletics tradition; no participation requirement.

cards.title: Spot the Paired Koʻo at Commencement
cards.subtitle: UH Mānoa commencement
cards.notes: During commencement, look for the paired ceremonial koʻo displayed before the stage rather than a conventional academic mace.
cards.short_summary: Two complementary Hawaiian ceremonial symbols replace the university’s former maces.
cards.evidence_claim: UH Mānoa states that paired male and female koʻo replaced old university maces in 2003 and are displayed before the degree-conferral stage.
cards.access_notes: Visible as part of official commencement proceedings.

cards.title: Save the Lei for After the Ceremony
cards.subtitle: UH Mānoa commencement etiquette
cards.notes: If celebrating a graduate, hold the lei until the ceremony has concluded; the commencement office identifies this as the traditional timing.
cards.short_summary: Graduates receive flower lei after, rather than during, the formal ceremony.
cards.evidence_claim: UH Mānoa commencement instructions state that flower lei traditionally are not presented or worn until after the ceremony.
cards.access_notes: Follow current commencement venue rules and ceremony instructions.

cards.title: Open Commencement with Chant and Protocol
cards.subtitle: Hawaiʻinuiākea School of Hawaiian Knowledge
cards.notes: Eligible graduates can join the voluntary chant and protocol that opens UH Mānoa commencement ceremonies with Hawaiʻinuiākea faculty and staff.
cards.short_summary: A voluntary Native Hawaiian protocol opens each campus commencement.
cards.evidence_claim: Hawaiʻinuiākea identifies the chant and protocol opportunity for its graduates and other Native Hawaiian graduates as a UH Mānoa tradition at each commencement.
cards.access_notes: Participation is voluntary and coordinated through Hawaiʻinuiākea for eligible graduates.

cards.title: Gather for Lā Hemo Kula
cards.subtitle: Hawaiʻinuiākea graduation celebration
cards.notes: For Hawaiʻinuiākea graduates and guests, plan for the separate eve-before graduation gathering, including its chant and protocol offering.
cards.short_summary: A distinct Hawaiʻinuiākea celebration takes place before campus commencement.
cards.evidence_claim: Hawaiʻinuiākea describes Lā Hemo Kula as graduation ceremonies held on the eve before UH Mānoa commencement and says chant and protocol are offered there for graduates and guests.
cards.access_notes: Guest reservations and participation details are set by Hawaiʻinuiākea.

cards.title: Begin Law School with the Pledge
cards.subtitle: William S. Richardson School of Law
cards.notes: New Richardson students encounter a formal pledge centered on preparation, service, integrity, rights, and justice at the start of legal study.
cards.short_summary: A Hawaiʻi Supreme Court chief justice has administered the orientation pledge to entering law classes.
cards.evidence_claim: Richardson Law reports that Chief Justice Mark Recktenwald administered the Law Student Pledge at orientation for 15 years, formally welcoming each entering class.
cards.source_title: Honoring the Service and Partnership of Chief Justice Recktenwald
cards.access_notes: Orientation ritual for entering Richardson Law students.

cards.title: Cheer the Etes and Bruzers
cards.subtitle: William S. Richardson School of Law
cards.notes: Follow the annual flag-football matchup between current women law students, the Etes, and alumnae, the Bruzers; official scores run through 2025.
cards.short_summary: This law-school rivalry began in 1978 and continues as an alumni-student tradition.
cards.evidence_claim: Richardson Law documents the Ete Bowl as a 40-plus-year tradition, begun in 1978, between Etes and Bruzers.
cards.access_notes: Participation and spectator details are organized by Richardson Law; play follows flag-football rules.

cards.title: Meet Faculty in Chef Hats on Stew Day
cards.subtitle: William S. Richardson School of Law
cards.notes: Day-program law students can watch for the pre-finals meal when faculty and staff serve stew, desserts, and recognition of student kindness.
cards.short_summary: Faculty-created Stew Day pairs a free meal with stories of students helping one another.
cards.evidence_claim: UH News reports that Stew Day is a Richardson Law tradition launched in 2004, with faculty and staff serving a no-cost meal to day-program students.
cards.source_title: UH Law School faculty, staff will serve hot meals to students as part of annual tradition
cards.access_notes: For full-time day JD students; offered by the law school around finals.

cards.title: Join Noodle Night at Twilight
cards.subtitle: William S. Richardson School of Law
cards.notes: Evening-program law students can watch for the faculty-and-staff-served Noodle Night meal, the companion ritual to daytime Stew Day.
cards.short_summary: The evening JD program has its own no-cost pre-finals meal and faculty service line.
cards.evidence_claim: UH News identifies Noodle Night as an annual Richardson Law tradition in which faculty and staff serve a no-cost meal to evening part-time students.
cards.source_title: UH Law School faculty, staff will serve hot meals to students as part of annual tradition
cards.access_notes: For Evening Part-Time Program students; traditionally scheduled around finals.

cards.title: Celebrate at FilGrad Mānoa
cards.subtitle: Center for Philippine Studies
cards.notes: Graduating Filipinx students can look for the annual FilGrad ceremony, built around cultural recognition, family, and student-organized celebration.
cards.short_summary: An annual, culturally centered graduation ceremony recognizes UH Mānoa’s Filipino community.
cards.evidence_claim: UH Mānoa’s Center for Philippine Studies calls FilGrad an annual tradition and lists the ninth annual event for May 15, 2026.
cards.access_notes: Participation is for graduating students and is coordinated by FilGrad and campus partners.
